title: Federal Judge Bars DOJ from Threatening Election Workers Ahead of Voting
snippet: A federal judge issued a temporary restraining order blocking the Justice Department from threatening local election officials with prosecution over voter eligibility disputes.
content:
A San Francisco federal judge has blocked the Justice Department from threatening state and local election workers with criminal prosecution, reining in a late-hour push by the Trump administration to influence how officials handle voter eligibility disputes.

Court Steps In Just Days Before Election

U.S. District Judge Trina Thompson issued the sweeping temporary restraining order on Friday in response to a lawsuit brought by the Service Employees International Union and voting rights advocacy groups. The directive orders federal officials to immediately cease demanding that local election personnel purge voter rolls, deny ballots to specific voters, or segregate cast votes based on claims of voter ineligibility.

"Because the public has a paramount interest in ensuring that election officials and workers are able to carry out their work in accordance with federal law and election procedure, and the official day of the Elections is only a couple of days away, the balance of the equities and public interest weigh in Plaintiffs' favor," wrote Thompson, an appointee of President Joe Biden.

Nationwide Impact and Mandated DOJ Action

The court's emergency intervention comes right after the Justice Department sent warning letters to election administrators across all 50 states, hinting at potential criminal charges regarding record preservation and voter qualifications. Under Judge Thompson's order, federal prosecutors must now contact all recipients of those letters and formally advise them that the threats and demands have been legally enjoined.

The Justice Department did not immediately respond to requests for comment regarding the ruling.

A Mounting Series of Legal Setbacks

Thompson's injunction follows similar rebukes from federal judges across the country. Earlier in the week, U.S. District Judge David Carter sternly rejected a Justice Department attempt to force California to isolate up to 20,000 ballots cast by suspected noncitizens, writing that "these threats must stop." The 9th Circuit Court of Appeals upheld Carter's decision on Friday.

Meanwhile, Chief District Judge James Boasberg in Washington, D.C., ordered the administration to share its list of disputed voters with an immigrant advocacy group, citing concerns that federal coercion was actively disrupting local election proceedings.
